To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the expression of cytochrome p450-dependent monooxyenases is similar in the horse and other laboratory and agricultural species, but the catalytic activity of these enzymes differs among the various species.
horses are more similar to laboratory species than to food producing species.
the horse has a low level of expression of cytochrome p450-dependent monooxgenases in its liver, and that this species is not suitable for studies on drug efficacy or on residue depletion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of cytochrome(s) P450 involved in the biocatalysis of xenobiotics in horse and other agricultural species.
the identification of cytochrome p450-dependent enzymes in the liver of the horse.
the comparative analysis of the biotransforming capacity of liver preparations from the horse and from other species of veterinary interest.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, although horses and cattle share many similarities in the metabolism of xenobiotics, they also have some differences.
, in the horse, cytochrome P-450-dependent biotransformation reactions occur, although with different kinetics and/or extent, when compared with other species.
horses should not be regarded as a model for any other species, including cattle, in terms of cytochrome-P450-dependent drug biotransformation and drug residue metabolism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the horse is a good model for the metabolism of xenobiotics, but it is not a good model for drug development.

the liver cytochrome(s) P450 involved in the metabolism of xenobiotics are similar in all species, and that the observed differences in the rates of metabolism are due to differences in the levels of expression of these enzymes.

the horse is an animal species that is not particularly different in its biotransformation profile when compared with the most common food-producing species, but is rather more similar to laboratory species.
The main takeaway from our work is that
horses, like other species, are not a good model to predict the metabolism of xenobiotics in other animals.
the horse is a suitable model for studies on drug efficacy, residue depletion, and toxicity in humans.
the use of horses as a model species for the evaluation of the pharmacokinetic properties of drugs in man is not justified.
